title: Matthew 22:41–46
context: Jesus turns the examination on the Pharisees: whose son is the Christ? Psalm 110:1 shows David calling the Messiah “Lord,” so the Son of David is more than a mere descendant. No one dares ask Him another question.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic Arminian and Reformed comment on Matthew 22:41–46, in the writers’ own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: How doth David then by the Spirit - By inspiration, call him Lord? If he be merely the son (or descendant) of David? If he be, as you suppose, a mere man, the son of a man? The Lord said to my Lord - This his dominion, to which David himself was subject, shows both the heavenly majesty of the king, and the nature of his kingdom.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 22:41–46)

reformed.quote: Mark and Luke express more clearly the reason why Christ put this question. It was because there prevailed among the scribes an erroneous opinion, that the promised Redeemer would be one of David's sons and successors, who would bring along with him nothing more elevated than human nature.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 22:41–46)

verses.text: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question,
verses.arminianNotes:
While they are still gathered, Jesus asks. The tested One becomes the examiner—grace that seeks their confession of the Messiah’s true identity.

Arminians hear invitation in the question. He draws them toward fuller light about who the Christ is, not merely to win a debate.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ seizes the moment of their gathering. The initiative shifts to the Son’s question.

God turns the tables on schedule. Revelation presses forward; their silence later will confirm the force of what He is about to show from Psalm 110.

verses.text: saying, “What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “Of David.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Whose son is the Christ?” They answer rightly as far as it goes: Son of David. Messianic hope tied to David’s line is true—and incomplete without Lordship.

Partial orthodoxy needs growth. Grace affirms Davidic descent and presses them to see more than ancestry.
verses.reformedNotes:
He asks what they think about the Christ; they reply the son of David. Jesus corrects their expectation of the covenant Messiah.

Scripture’s promise of David’s son stands. Jesus will deepen it—Messiah is David’s son and David’s Lord by God’s design.

verses.text: He said to them, “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
David, “in the Spirit,” calls Him Lord. Inspiration matters: the psalm is Spirit-given, not mere poetry. The Messiah’s identity rests on God’s Word.

Classical Arminians urge Spirit-taught Scripture reading. Grace opens Psalm 110 so hearers may confess Christ’s lordship freely and truly.
verses.reformedNotes:
“In the Spirit” marks David’s speech as God-breathed prophecy. The argument hangs on inspired Scripture.

The Spirit spoke through David. Christ’s lordship over David is not later invention but revelatory fact embedded in the psalm.

verses.text: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, sit on my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’?
verses.arminianNotes:
Psalm 110:1: Yahweh speaks to David’s Lord—seat at the right hand, enemies underfoot. Exaltation and victory belong to the Messiah.

The risen Christ invites trust and allegiance. Enemies subdued is promise; sitting at God’s right hand summons present worship, not only future hope.
verses.reformedNotes:
Double “Lord”: Yahweh addresses David’s Lord with session at the right hand and promised conquest.

This is the Messiah’s divine-royal status and certain triumph. God’s decree seats the Son and guarantees His enemies’ subjection.
verses.keyContrast: Both receive Psalm 110 as Messianic exaltation. Arminians typically highlight the summons to trust and worship the enthroned Lord; Reformed Christians emphasize the same text as God’s sovereign decree seating Christ and securing His victory.

verses.text: “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?”
verses.arminianNotes:
If David calls Him Lord, how is He David’s son? Both are true: descent and superior Lordship. The riddle pushes beyond a merely human heir.

Arminian readers welcome the tension as revelation: Jesus is Son of David and Lord—worthy of the faith the Pharisees still withhold.
verses.reformedNotes:
The question locks the dilemma: Lord and son together. Genealogy alone cannot explain Psalm 110.

Reformed christology in seed form: the Messiah shares David’s line and transcends David as Lord. God has spoken; the Christ must be confessed accordingly.
verses.keyContrast: Both hold Son-of-David and Lord together. Arminians typically emphasize the call to confess this fuller Christ in living faith; Reformed Christians stress the same identity as God-revealed truth that silences inadequate Messianic reductions.

verses.text: No one was able to answer him a word, neither did any man dare ask him any more questions from that day forward.
verses.arminianNotes:
Silence can be conviction’s doorway—or mere retreat from an uncomfortable Lord.

Grace gave clarity about the Christ. The right response is not only stopped mouths but opened faith in David’s Son and Lord.
verses.reformedNotes:
They cannot answer; questioning ceases. Christ’s wisdom closes the trap cycle.

God ends the examination on His Son’s terms. Silence does not equal salvation, yet it marks the public defeat of their tests as the path to the cross continues under divine purpose.
